questions.q: Is it an EP?
choices: No; a faded day, a watch at most
Yes; the gap held, so it counts
Yes; buy the close, the gap is support
No; the day's volume was too light
questions.story: An 18.1% earnings gap on 4.6x volume. The day never trades back to the prior close, but it closes at 32% of its range.
questions.answer: No; a faded day, a watch at most
questions.why: No. The gap held, but the day closed at 32% of its range and the rule is the upper half. A faded gap day is not an EP. At most it goes on the list as a delayed-reaction watch. The would-be close buy at 109.88 was stopped for 0.0R.
questions.lesson_line: The gap held and the buyers left. That is a watch, not a buy.

wrong.Yes; buy the close, the gap is support: The would-be close buy at 109.88 was stopped. A held gap with a weak close is not an EP.
wrong.Yes; the gap held, so it counts: Holding the gap is one gate. Closing in the upper half is another, and this fails it.
wrong.No; the day's volume was too light: 4.6x is well over the 3 times floor. The close is what fails.

questions.simple: It is not an EP, because the day closed at 32% of its range and the rule needs the upper half.

deeper.trap: MU, 2024-09-26: the gap held, since the low of 107.53 stayed above the prior close of 95.77, so a quick look says EP. The close at 32% of the range says the buyers left. Both gates must pass: the gap holds and the close is in the upper half.

reasons: fixed before

questions.q: Take the day-2 break?
choices: No; the buy is under the 200-day
No; the 66% close is too weak to buy
Yes; the gap and volume qualify
Yes; the 200-day is about to turn up
questions.story: A stock down 17% over six months gaps 12.1% on earnings on 3.6x, closing at 66%. The day-2 break would fill at 161.21. The 200-day sits at 168.35.
questions.answer: No; the buy is under the 200-day
questions.why: No. No longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless the trade is a parabolic long. The day-2 break would fill at 161.21, under the 200-day at 168.35. The gap and the volume passed. The location failed.
questions.lesson_line: Neglected stocks often live under the 200-day. No long until price is over it.

wrong.Yes; the gap and volume qualify: The gap day passed. The location failed: no longs below the 200-day.
wrong.Yes; the 200-day is about to turn up: The rule is price above the 200-day at the buy, not an average that may turn later.
wrong.No; the 66% close is too weak to buy: A 66% close is in the upper half, which passes. Only the top quarter is a grade cue, and that is not a gate.

questions.simple: No. We do not buy long below the 200-day average, and this buy at 161.21 would sit under it at 168.35.

deeper.trap: Neglected stocks often live under the 200-day, so this rule can say no to a gap that looks perfect. The test is price at the buy, not the picture of the gap day. AMZN, 2022-02-04: a 12.1% gap on 3.6x, closed at 66%, and the break at 161.21 was stopped, 0.0R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)
a held decision (D-020)

questions.q: EP or Power Earnings Gap?
choices: A PEG; not neglected
An EP; the gap and volume are A+
An EP; 25.5% is close enough
Neither; a leader cannot gap
questions.story: A software leader near its highs gaps 16.6% on earnings on 11.2x volume, closing at 80%. It was up 25.5% over the prior 126 sessions and 19.3% over the prior 63.
questions.answer: A PEG; not neglected
questions.why: A Power Earnings Gap. Up 25.5% over 126 sessions and 19.3% over 63; the neglect line is at most 25% and 15%. An established leader at highs gapping on a report is the PEG.
questions.lesson_line: A leader at highs gapping on earnings is a PEG. Measure the six months to know.

wrong.An EP; the gap and volume are A+: The day is A+ for either setup. The stock before it decides, and it was not neglected.
wrong.An EP; 25.5% is close enough: Close enough is over, and the 63-session line fails by more. Measured, not eyeballed.
wrong.Neither; a leader cannot gap: Leaders gap on reports all the time. That is the PEG.

questions.q: Bought at 227.60, stop 224.95. You sell a third at 235.55. How many R did that third bank?
questions.why: 3R. The gain divided by the fill minus the stop. ENPH got there the session after the day-3 entry.
questions.lesson_line: Count every exit in R. The first third is 3R.
questions.simple: Divide the gain per share by the risk per share. Selling at 235.55 banks 3R.

deeper.trap: The 3R belongs to the third you sold. The other two thirds are still open, so the whole trade has not banked 3R yet. Count each exit in R on the shares it covered.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, first trim)

questions.q: By our rules, how do you take profit on the way up?
choices: A third at 3R, a third at 5R, trail
Everything at 3R, the first target
Nothing; hold all of it for the big run
Half at 3R, the other half at 5R
questions.story: A news EP after the election: a 14.2% gap on 3.9x, the day-3 break bought at 259.70, stop 257.10. It reaches 3R the next session and later 34R.
questions.answer: A third at 3R, a third at 5R, trail
questions.why: A third at 3R, a third at 5R, and the last third on the 10-day trail, sold on a close below it. COIN reached 3R the next session and later 34R. It gave its gains back in December after 34R, so the trims mattered. The plan is adjustable, but 3R and 5R are the default.
questions.lesson_line: Sell partials into strength. An EP that gives it all back only hurts the untrimmed.

wrong.Everything at 3R, the first target: Selling everything in the first day or two and missing the multi-week trend is a named mistake. A third at 3R, not all of it.
wrong.Nothing; hold all of it for the big run: The plan trims: a third at 3R and another third at 5R. COIN gave its gains back in December after 34R, so the trims mattered.
wrong.Half at 3R, the other half at 5R: The plan sells thirds, not halves, and keeps the last third on a trail instead of selling it at 5R.

questions.simple: Our plan sells a third at 3R and another third at 5R, then trails the last third.

deeper.trap: The 34R figure is a trap. It was the peak, not a plan. A third is sold at 3R, a third at 5R, and the last third trails, so that part can give gains back.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)
the owner often waits for 5R on the first trim

questions.q: What kept this trade a win?
choices: The trims and the 10-day trail
Holding the original stop
Widening the stop to give it room
Selling everything at 3R
questions.story: You bought the day-3 break at 227.60, stop 224.95. 3R came the next session. Weeks later the stock tops, rolls over and collapses through your original stop.
questions.answer: The trims and the 10-day trail
questions.why: The trims and the 10-day trail. A third comes off at 3R and a third at 5R. The last third trails the 10-day while the stock moves fast. This stock topped and collapsed through the original stop, so a plan with only that stop gives the move back. It was ENPH, bought 2021-10-29 at 227.60, and its best run reached 20.7R.
questions.lesson_line: Fast movers get the 10-day. By the time the stop is hit, two thirds are gone.

wrong.Holding the original stop: Holding only the original stop means the whole position exits at the stop, so the gain is given back.
wrong.Selling everything at 3R: A third comes off at 3R. Selling everything misses the run to 20.7R and the multi-week trend.
wrong.Widening the stop to give it room: The stop only moves up, never down or wider. A looser stop does not bank anything.

questions.simple: The trims and the 10-day trail kept it a win, because they banked gains before the stock fell through the stop.

deeper.example: ENPH: the buy was 227.60 with the stop at 224.95, only 1.2% away, and 3R came the next session. Later the stock topped and collapsed through that stop, yet its best run reached 20.7R. A plan with trims banked part of that run. A plan with one stop gave it back.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E51, E52 and B19)
held decision D-024 (the trail line)

questions.q: Hold through the report?
choices: No; hold through only if up 5R
No; hold through only if up 3R
Yes; the last report was a surprise
Yes; sell half and hold the rest
questions.story: Your EP from last quarter's report is up 2R. The next report is tomorrow after the close.
questions.answer: No; hold through only if up 5R

questions.lesson_line: The next report is a gap you cannot stop. Five R buys the ticket.

wrong.Yes; the last report was a surprise: A past surprise does not lower the risk of the next report. The rule is up 5R or not held.
wrong.No; hold through only if up 3R: 3R is the first-trim level. The hold-through line is 5R.
wrong.Yes; sell half and hold the rest: Half the position still goes through the report at 2R, far under the 5R line.

questions.simple: No. We hold through a report only when the trade is up 5R, and this one is up 2R.

deeper.trap: The rule has two halves. No new buys in the 3 days before a report. Hold through one only if up 5R. Do not mix them up.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)
one cited fact only

Pass; a 15% gap is too big to buy
Buy it; EPs often beat a weak market

questions.q: What is the trade?

Pass; three days is too late to buy
Buy it; stop under the gap-day low
Wait for the gap-day high to break

questions.q: Write the plan: entry, stop, first trim.
choices: Market 52.00; stop 51.55; third at 3R
Limit 51.40; stop 51.15; third at 3R
Market 52.00; stop 51.40; all out at 3R
Limit 51.60; stop 51.55; half at 3R

questions.answer: Market 52.00; stop 51.55; third at 3R

questions.q: By the card's cues: A+, A, B or B-?
choices: A+; record volume on a neglected name
B-; the gap is over 25% and too big
A; record volume is just a grading cue
B; the close is only 82% of the range
questions.story: A stock sideways-to-down for a year, with no earlier EP, gaps 20.3% on earnings on 27.6x volume. That is the highest volume on its chart by far. It closes at 82%.
questions.answer: A+; record volume on a neglected name
questions.why: A+. The highest volume in years is our A+ volume cue, and 27.6x is far past the 5 times line. The stock drifted sideways to down for a year, the neglect the setup needs. The close at 82% is in the top quarter. Bonde cautions at gaps over 20%, but the card's line is 25%, and this gap is 20.3%.
questions.lesson_line: Record volume on a forgotten stock is the loudest EP there is.

wrong.B-; the gap is over 25% and too big: The grade-down line on our card is 25%. This gap is 20.3%, under it.
wrong.A; record volume is just a grading cue: It is a cue, and cues set the grade. Record volume is the A+ row.
wrong.B; the close is only 82% of the range: 82% is in the top quarter, the grade-up cue. Nothing here grades down.

questions.simple: A+. Record volume on a stock that drifted for a year is our top volume cue, and nothing here grades it down.

deeper.trap: Do not read the grade as a forecast. Volume is a cue that sets the grade and the size. DLB is the loudest case here and ran 17.1R, but a high grade promises nothing about the next one.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line (ep.volume_ideal)
Bonde's 20% caution differs from the card's 25%
grading is discretionary (E50), so the stem asks for the card's cues

questions.q: What do you do on day five?
choices: Hold; the stop and the clock decide
Sell; five flat days is a failed trade
Move the stop up to breakeven right now
Hold, but add as it builds a base
questions.story: A news gap of 12.1% on 10.3x. You bought the day-2 break at 94.17, stop 93.17. Five days later it has gone nowhere, still above the stop.
questions.answer: Hold; the stop and the clock decide
questions.why: Hold. The stop is the exit, and the time stop sells a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days. At day five neither has fired. SIG stalled a week above the stop and reached 3R on day 8, a patient trade that paid. Bonde's stricter 5-day clock is his rule, not ours.
questions.lesson_line: Sideways above the stop is not a loss. Let the rules, not boredom, make the exit.

wrong.Sell; five flat days is a failed trade: Bonde used 5 days. Our time stop is 10 trading days under 1R.
wrong.Move the stop up to breakeven right now: Breakeven comes at 2R to 5R, ideally. This trade has not moved.
wrong.Hold, but add as it builds a base: The full size goes in at one price with one stop. No adding.

questions.simple: Hold. A trade still under 1R is sold after 10 trading days, and at day five the stop is not hit.

deeper.trap: Patience has a limit. SIG reached 3R on day 8, but the same flat picture past day 10 and under 1R means sell. The stop and the clock are the rules, not a hunch that it will go.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33, time stop)
ours and Bonde's clocks differ

questions.q: Hidden ticker; the gap day is the last bar. Read the months before it and the gap day. Buy a delayed break, or pass?
choices: Take it; neglect, strong close
Pass; the stock was already up
Pass; the gap day closed weak
Take it, but after the gap fills
questions.answer: Take it; neglect, strong close
questions.why: Take it. The months before the gap show a stock down 19% over six months, the neglect the setup needs. The gap day closed near its high, at 85% of its range. A break over the post-gap high is the delayed trigger, and this one came on day 4. The real numbers: a 10.5% gap on 7.4x volume.
questions.lesson_line: Months of nothing, then a gap that holds. That is the picture to memorise.

wrong.Pass; the stock was already up: Look left: the stock was down 19% over six months. That is the neglect the EP needs.
wrong.Pass; the gap day closed weak: The gap day closed at 85% of its range, in the top quarter. The close passes.
wrong.Take it, but after the gap fills: A trade back to the prior close fills the gap and ends the setup. We step aside then, we do not buy.

questions.simple: Take it. The stock was down for months, then gapped and closed near its high, so a delayed break is a valid buy.

deeper.trap: Look left before you look at the gap. A prior run-up, a weak close or a gap that fills would change the answer.

reasons: rests on the dossier's chart read (d07)
a card line (ep.neglect)

questions.q: Hidden ticker; the gap day is the last bar. The prior close was up 25.5% over 126 sessions and 19.3% over 63. EP or pass?
choices: Pass; up into the news, a PEG
Take it; the gap day is A+
Take it; 25.5% is close enough
Pass; the gap day closed too weak
questions.answer: Pass; up into the news, a PEG
questions.why: Pass as an EP. The stock was up 25.5% over 126 sessions and 19.3% over 63, and our neglect line is at most 25% and 15%. An established leader at highs gapping on a report is a Power Earnings Gap, not an EP. The gap day itself was strong, with 11.2x volume and a close at 80% of its range. This was CRM on 2020-08-26.
questions.lesson_line: A big gap on a leader at highs is a PEG. The six months before say so.

wrong.Take it; the gap day is A+: The gap day itself is strong, with 11.2x volume and a close at 80% of its range. The stock before it was up into the news, which is the PEG lesson's trade.
wrong.Take it; 25.5% is close enough: Close enough is over the line, and the 63-session number misses by more. The line is measured, not eyeballed.
wrong.Pass; the gap day closed too weak: The gap day closed at 80% of its range, in the upper half. The close passes and the neglect is what fails.

questions.simple: Pass as an EP. It was up 25.5% over 126 sessions, past the 25% neglect limit, so it is a PEG.

deeper.trap: CRM missed the neglect line by a small margin: 25.5% against 25% over 126 sessions and 19.3% against 15% over 63. A near-miss still fails. The gap day was strong, which is why it looks tempting. Check the six months before the gap first.

reasons: held decision D-002 (earnings gap on a neglected or an established name)
numbers from our own dossier scan
neglect line is a proposed card line

questions.q: After a delayed-entry buy, the stop can be moved down to the gap-day low.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up, never down or wider. The delayed entry's stop is a few cents under the trigger day's low, and it moves up from there. Every position has a real stop order with the broker.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is an appointment, not a debate.
questions.simple: False, because the stop only moves up. Moving it down to the gap-day low would widen it.

deeper.trap: There is one exception, and it is not about nerve. If a stock gaps down through the stop, the low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop. If the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, the stop only moves up)

questions.q: On our card, a gap day must close in the top quarter of its range to count as an EP.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The gate is a close in the upper half of the range. A close in the top quarter is a grade cue, not a gate. It helps the grade, but a close in the upper half still counts.
questions.lesson_line: Upper half is the gate. Top quarter is a grade cue.
questions.simple: False, because the gap day only has to close in the upper half of its range, and the top quarter is a grade cue.

reasons: card gate versus grade cue

questions.q: If an EP opens above your 3R level, you take that trim at the open.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. If a stock opens above a trim level, 3R or 5R, take that trim at the open. It applies to every trim level, not only 3R.
questions.lesson_line: Gap past a trim level: take it at the open.
questions.simple: True. If the open is already past a trim level, we sell that trim right at the open.

reasons: one cited fact only
rests on the owner's rulebook (F63)

questions.q: Average daily volume is 2,000,000 shares. By 10:00 the stock has traded 1,500,000. What multiple of average is that?
questions.why: 0.75 times. Divide the 1,500,000 shares traded by the 2,000,000 average. Our card wants the full average daily volume traded within the first 30 minutes. Anything under a full day's average means the volume is not there, so the day-one buy is off.
questions.lesson_line: Short of a full day's volume by 10:00 means no day-one buy.
questions.simple: 1,500,000 divided by 2,000,000 is 0.75, so the stock has not traded a full average day by 10:00.

reasons: computed key
card line is proposed

questions.q: What do you do about the day-one buy?
choices: Skip it; the volume is not there
Take it; holding the gap is enough
Half now and half at the close
Buy the close if it holds the gap
questions.story: A stock gaps up on earnings and holds the gap. At 10:00 it has traded only a fifth of its average daily volume.
questions.answer: Skip it; the volume is not there
questions.why: Skip it. On our card, the full average daily volume must trade within the first 30 minutes. A fifth of it is far short. Without that crowd the day-one buy is off, and a held gap alone does not rescue it. Kullamagi: volume is the number one thing.
questions.lesson_line: No crowd in the first 30 minutes, no day-one buy.

wrong.Take it; holding the gap is enough: Volume is the number one thing. A held gap without the crowd can still fill.
wrong.Half now and half at the close: Splitting the buy does not fix missing volume. We buy the full size once, at one price.
wrong.Buy the close if it holds the gap: Our day-one buy is an opening-range buy with the volume on pace, not a close buy.

questions.simple: Skip the day-one buy, because only a fifth of a normal day's volume traded by 10:00 and the crowd is not there.

reasons: reworded before

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We make no new buys in the ___ days before an earnings report.
questions.why: 3. We make no new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report. A report can gap the stock right through your stop.
questions.simple: We make no new buys in the 3 days before a report. The report can gap the stock right through your stop.
questions.lesson_line: No new buys in the 3 days before a report. A report is a gap you cannot stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: On our card, selling the whole position in the first day or two is a named mistake.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Our card names it: selling everything in the first day or two and missing the multi-week trend. We take a third at 3R, another third at 5R, then trail the last third.
questions.lesson_line: Do not sell it all in the first day or two. Trim by the plan and trail the rest.
questions.simple: True, because selling everything early misses the multi-week trend, so we trim in thirds and trail the last third.

reasons: named mistake on the card; stable
